Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
As a city council member, Rohini was no stranger to the inner workings of her community. But it wasn't until the devastating nightclub fire that ravaged the downtown area two years ago, killing 15 people and injuring dozens more, that she began to see the world through a different lens. She had been attending a charity event at the club that night, and as she watched in horror as flames engulfed the building, she knew her life would never be the same. In the aftermath of the fire, Rohini found herself increasingly preoccupied with thoughts of danger lurking around every corner. She became convinced that the world was a treacherous place, where catastrophe could strike at any moment. As she went about her daily routine, she began to notice things she had never paid attention to before – the emergency exits in buildings, the proximity of fire alarms, the potential escape routes from crowded spaces. At night, Rohini's anxiety spiked, and she found it harder to feel safe than during the day. She would lie awake for hours, her mind racing with worst-case scenarios, as she mentally rehearsed evacuation plans and identified potential hiding spots in case of an emergency. Her friends and family grew concerned about her newfound hypervigilance, but Rohini couldn't shake off the feeling that she needed to be on guard all the time. As a council member, Rohini's job required her to attend public events and meet with constituents, but she found herself avoiding unfamiliar places and situations that put her body under physical stress. She stopped attending late-night meetings and began to limit her public appearances, citing "scheduling conflicts" as an excuse. Her colleagues noticed the change in her behavior, but Rohini couldn't bring herself to explain why she felt so uneasy. Rohini's constant scanning of her environment for signs of threat became a habitual behavior, one that she performed without even realizing it. She would walk into a room and immediately scan the exits, identify potential escape routes, and notice any suspicious-looking individuals. Her friends began to comment on how "jumpy" she seemed, always looking over her shoulder or glancing around nervously. As time passed, Rohini's avoidance behaviors took a toll on her relationships and daily life. She stopped attending social gatherings and started turning down invitations to speak at community events. Her colleagues began to question her commitment to her role as council member, and Rohini found herself feeling isolated and alone. It wasn't until she received a concerned phone call from her best friend, expressing worry about Rohini's increasingly reclusive behavior, that she realized she needed help. As Rohini looked in the mirror, she saw a person she barely recognized – someone who was constantly on edge, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. She knew it was time to seek professional help, not just to overcome her symptoms but to reclaim her sense of purpose and confidence. As Rohini sat in her therapist's office, she felt a mix of emotions: fear, anxiety, and hope. She was terrified of confronting the memories of that fateful night, but she was also desperate to break free from the prison of hypervigilance and avoidance behaviors that had consumed her life for so long. With a deep breath, she began to tell her story, hoping that by facing her fears head-on, she could finally find some peace.
